current_episode.title: Your Brain Is Hiding the Truth From You (#314)

guest.titre: Journalist, Harvard and Berkeley Professor, and Author
guest.bio_context: Michael Pollan is a journalist and professor at both Harvard and Berkeley who has spent his career following deceptively simple questions to their strangest and deepest roots. His new book, A World Appears: A Journey Into Consciousness, explores the question of why we experience anything at all. He is known for making complex scientific and philosophical topics accessible to general audiences.

context.real_quote: Consciousness is precious, consciousness is under siege, and consciousness is worth defending.
key_stats: The human brain weighs just 3 pounds yet consumes 20% of the body's total metabolic energy
The brain generates only enough electricity to power a small lightbulb
Thomas Nagel published his essay 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' in the 1970s

context.transcript_excerpt: A brain weighs just 3 pounds, yet it consumes a massive 20% of our metabolic energy. It generates only enough electricity to power a small lightbulb. Yet it does something no lightbulb, no supercomputer, and no chatbot has ever managed to do. It makes a world appear. Colors, sounds, the feeling of being you. How does it do this? Hi everyone, I'm Lynne Tomin and this is 3 Takeaways. On 3 Takeaways, I talk with some of the world's best thinkers, business leaders, writers, politicians, newsmakers, and scientists. Each episode ends with 3 key takeaways to help us understand the world, and maybe even ourselves a little better. Today I'm excited to be with Michael Pollan, a journalist, Harvard and Berkeley professor, and author who spent his career following one deceptively simple question after another to their strangest, deepest roots. In his new book, A World Appears, A Journey Into Consciousness, he's chasing the biggest question of all, not what we think, but why we experience anything at all. Welcome Michael, and thanks so much for joining 3 Takeaways today. Thank you Lynne, good to be here. Great to be with you. The word consciousness is not easy to define. Can you define it simply for us? What is consciousness? I define it simply as subjective experience, which you could even shorten to experience. The fact that you have experience or awareness is another good definition. I also like the definition that Thomas Nagel, the NYU philosopher, put forward back in the 70s. He wrote a wonderful essay called What Is It Like to Be a Bat? And even though we don't know exactly what it's like to be a bat, to navigate the world using sonar rather than light, we know it's like something to do that. And so therefore, we must concede the bat is conscious. Your toaster, on the other hand, does not have experience. There is nothing it is like to be your toaster, I'm pretty sure. It is such an interesting framing. What is it like to be a bat? Yeah, it is. He's a philosopher, but his definition is really caught on with a lot of the neuroscientists. What are the major mysteries around consciousness and why aren't they easy to resolve? The biggest mystery is why we have it. Our brain does a lot of work without our consciousness, without our awareness. It is working all the time to monitor what's going on in your body. It's taking in information from the environment and performing computations and making changes based on that information. It does so much without consciousness. Consciousness is like the tip of an iceberg. So the question arises, why do we need it? Why isn't everything automated? Why aren't we more like zombies? We don't know the answer. I mean, you can point to some adaptive value in being conscious. One theory that I found compelling is that for humans who are profoundly social creatures, we depend on other people to survive. You need to navigate a very complex social reality where you need to be able to predict what other people are going to do, what they're going to say. And that is so complex that you couldn't automate all the variables involved. So consciousness is necessitated by our identity as social beings. As to why it's so difficult to study, I think the big problem is that we can't step outside it. All our science, all our speculation, what we're doing now, all takes place within this bubble of consciousness. There is no ability to stand outside and acquire a kind of God's eye view or view from nowhere and really see it whole. So I think that that definitely complicates our efforts to understand consciousness. And we just may not be smart enough. One leading theory says that consciousness is like a dark theater with a single spotlight stage, the global workspace. Can you explain that metaphor? This is a very popular theory of consciousness. pending_qa.q: Are animals other than humans conscious, and how far does consciousness extend in the animal kingdom?
pending_qa.r: Pollan notes that many mammals, several bird species, and octopuses are now thought by some scientists to be conscious, with some extending that circle even to insects. He argues that consciousness likely begins with feelings originating in the upper brain stem rather than the cortex, meaning any creature capable of feeling must be granted consciousness, though he remains uncertain about insects, protozoa, and bacteria.

pending_qa.q: Is artificial intelligence conscious or sentient?
pending_qa.r: Pollan does not exclude the possibility that AI could become sentient in the future, but he currently believes AI lacks genuine feelings and the embodied mortality that gives weight to feelings. He distinguishes AI's outputs as 'simulated feelings' rather than real ones, and notes that AI is trained on human culture — itself once removed from the real world — rather than on the world humans actually inhabit.

pending_qa.q: What is the difference between sentience and consciousness according to Michael Pollan?
pending_qa.r: Pollan defines sentience as the ability to sense changes in one's environment, evaluate whether they are good or bad, and take appropriate action — a simpler, foundational form that may be a property of all living things, including plants. Consciousness, by contrast, is a more developed form built on top of sentience, involving subjective experience and feelings.

pending_qa.q: Are plants sentient despite having no brain or nervous system?
pending_qa.r: Pollan believes plants are sentient, drawing on research showing they remember, decide, and respond to their environment. He argues sentience — the ability to sense environmental changes, evaluate them, and respond — may be a property of all living things, as relying solely on instinct to navigate a constantly changing world seems far-fetched.

pending_qa.q: What are Michael Pollan's three key takeaways about consciousness?
pending_qa.r: Pollan's three takeaways are that consciousness is precious, that consciousness is under siege, and that consciousness is worth defending.
